Codenamed Operation Neptune and preceded by the elaborate deception Operation Bodyguard, this June 6, 1944 assault is the largest seaborne invasion in history — by what more common name is it known?
Normandy landings: World War II landing operation in Europe.
After resigning as Germany's finance minister within six months of taking office, this politician later co-founded a left-wing party opposing his former party's reforms — who is he?
Forced out of school at ten by poverty, this future Chinese general rose from private second class to become Minister of National Defense from 1954 to 1959 — who was he?
Peng Dehuai: Chinese politician and general (1898–1974)

Ruling Mexico for more than three decades until his 1911 overthrow, this general-turned-dictator once studied for the priesthood before switching to law under the mentorship of future president Benito Juárez. Who is he?
Porfirio Díaz: President and Dictator of Mexico from 1876 to 1911.
A trained psychiatrist who became the first president of Republika Srpska, he spent twelve years as a fugitive before being convicted of genocide by a UN tribunal — who is he?
Radovan Karadžić: Bosnian Serb politician and war criminal (born 1945)
This Congress politician led his party to victory in the 2023 election and became the second Chief Minister of Telangana — who is he?
Revanth Reddy: Chief Minister of Telangana (born 1969)
Raised in Russian-ruled Poland in a secular Jewish family, this Marxist theorist co-founded the anti-war Spartacus League and is remembered as a champion of socialist democracy — who is she?
A Harvard graduate and second cousin to a future U.S. president, this Boston revolutionary founded the Sons of Liberty and signed the Declaration of Independence — who was he?
Samuel Adams: Founding Father of the United States (1722–1803)
Rising through the ranks despite the Great Purge of the 1930s, this Soviet officer became a Marshal of the Soviet Union and led the Ukrainian Front during the 1939 invasion of Poland — who is he?

As part of the Battle of the Bulge, this December 1944 clash saw the 101st Airborne help defend a vital Belgian crossroads town where seven main roads converged, blocking the German drive toward Antwerp — which engagement is this?

Siege of Bastogne: American/German engagement December 1944. Until 23 December, the weather prevented Allied aircraft from attempting to resupply Bastogne or from performing ground attack missions against German forces.

On 26 September 1983, this Soviet duty officer judged his early-warning system's report of incoming U.S. missiles to be a false alarm — disobeying protocol and likely averting nuclear war. Who was he?
Stanislav Petrov: Soviet Air Defence Forces officer (1939–2017)
Nicknamed for both his towering height and his 23-year run, this architect of the 'Swedish Model' welfare state holds the record as his country's longest-serving prime minister — who was he?
Tage Erlander: Prime Minister of Sweden from 1946 to 1969.
Of African descent through his mother, this French Revolutionary Wars general was one of only a handful of men of color to command European troops as a general officer in that era — who is he?
This Mitsubishi engineer had the extraordinarily unlucky distinction of being caught in both the Hiroshima and Nagasaki atomic bombings in August 1945 — and lived to tell about it. Who is he?
Tsutomu Yamaguchi: Japanese atomic bombing survivor.

This King of Italy also claimed the titles Emperor of Ethiopia and King of the Albanians after Italy's invasions of those countries, and reigned through the entire rise and fall of the Fascist regime — who was he?
Victor Emmanuel III: King of Italy from 1900 to 1946.

Launched as Operation Enduring Freedom in response to the 9/11 attacks, this two-decade conflict began by toppling the Taliban-ruled Islamic Emirate with help from the Northern Alliance — what was it?
War in Afghanistan (2001–2021): U.S Armed conflict in South Asia.
A descendant of the Viking Rollo and once called 'the Bastard,' this Duke of Normandy won the Battle of Hastings in 1066 and became the first Norman king of England — who was he?
William the Conqueror: King of England from 1066 to 1087.

A former prosecutor general, he served the shortest term of any elected leader in his country's democratic history before removal in 2025 — and is now serving life for leading an insurrection. Which South Korean president is it?
Yoon Suk Yeol: President of South Korea from 2022 to 2025.
Which of these four was born earliest?
John Ray (born 1627) is the earliest of the four. John Ray (29 November 1627 – 17 January 1705) was an English Christian naturalist and one of the earliest English parson-naturalists.
Which of these four was born earliest?
Henry Vaughan (born 1621) is the earliest of the four. Henry Vaughan (1621 – 23 April 1695) was a Welsh metaphysical poet, author and translator writing in English, and a medical physician.
Which of these four began earliest?
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four dates back furthest?
Lisp (programming language) (founded 1958) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below is best known as a physicist?
John Theophilus Desaguliers is a physicist. Desaguliers's most important patron was James Brydges, 1st Duke of Chandos.
Which of these four is a chemist?
Otto Hahn is a chemist. Otto Hahn (German: [ˈɔtoː ˈhaːn]; 8 March 1879 – 28 July 1968) was a German chemist who was a pioneer in the field of radiochemistry.
What is the atomic number of Californium?
Californium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Cf and atomic number 98.
In what year was Mohamed Atta born?
Mohamed Atta: In Hamburg, Atta attended prayers at the al-Quds Mosque where he met Marwan al-Shehhi, Ramzi bin al-Shibh, and Ziad Jarrah, with whom he formed the Hamburg cell.
In what year was Rakesh Sharma born?
Rakesh Sharma (born 13 January 1949) is an Indian cosmonaut and a pilot of the Indian Air Force.
In what year was Mikhail Lomonosov born?
Mikhail Lomonosov: One of the founders of modern geology, Lomonosov was also a poet and influenced the formation of the modern Russian literary language.
In what year did Hamish Harding die?
Hamish Harding: George Hamish Livingston Harding (24 June 1964 – 18 June 2023) was a British businessman, pilot and adventurer based in the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
In what year did Manmohan Singh die?
Manmohan Singh: A member of the Indian National Congress, Singh was the first and remains the only Sikh prime minister of India.
In what year was Plutonium discovered?
Plutonium is a chemical element; it has symbol Pu and atomic number 94.
In what year was Tungsten discovered?
Tungsten (also called wolfram) is a chemical element; it has symbol W (from German: Wolfram) and atomic number 74.
Ilyushin Il-96: Voronezh Aircraft Production Association. It is powered by four high-bypass Aviadvigatel PS-90 twin-spool turbofan engines.
In which country is Dassault Mirage 2000?
Dassault Mirage 2000: France. Work on what would become the Mirage 2000 originated with the "Delta 1000" project launched in 1972.
Who is credited with discovering Horologium?

Horologium (constellation): Nicolas Louis de Lacaille. It was first described by the French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille in 1756 and visualized by him as a clock with a pendulum and a second hand.
Who is credited with discovering Hubble's law?
Hubble's law: Georges Lemaître. The Friedmann equations showed the universe might be expanding, and presented the expansion speed if that were the case.
Who is credited with discovering Eris?
Eris (dwarf planet): Michael E. Brown. Eris (minor-planet number 136199) is the most massive and second-largest known dwarf planet in the Solar System.
Hiding in coffee, fresh bread, and ripe fruit, this aldehyde is also what your liver makes when breaking down alcohol — and a prime culprit behind the morning-after hangover. What is it?
Acetaldehyde (IUPAC systematic name ethanal) is an organic chemical compound with the formula CH3CH=O.
This exaggerated immune reaction causes the body to mistake a harmless substance for a threat, triggering symptoms from a runny nose to a full anaphylactic reaction — what is it?
Allergy is an exaggerated immune response where the body mistakenly identifies an ordinarily harmless allergen as a threat.

Its name means 'unlike other shrimp.' Known best from the Burgess Shale, this extinct radiodont swam with body flaps and stared out through huge compound eyes packed with lenses — what was this stem-arthropod?

Anomalocaris (from Ancient Greek, meaning "anomalous", and, meaning "shrimp", with the intended meaning "unlike other shrimp") is an extinct genus of radiodont, an order of early-diverging stem-group marine arthropods.

Caused by the parasitic roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides, this infection hides in plain sight — over 85% of cases have no symptoms at all — yet in children it can stunt weight gain and trigger learning problems. What's the disease called?
Ascariasis is a disease caused by the parasitic roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides. The eggs hatch in the intestines, the larvae burrow through the gut wall, and migrate to the lungs via the blood.
Facing a shortage of staff, this American lawyer volunteered himself as chief prosecutor at the Einsatzgruppen trial at Nuremberg and later championed an International Criminal Court — who was he?
Ben Ferencz (March 11, 1920 - April 7, 2023) was an American lawyer.
This leafy vegetable forms no head, just green blades atop pale bulbous stalks, with a flavor often compared to a mix of spinach and water chestnut — what vegetable is it?

Bok choy (American English, Canadian English, and Australian English), pak choi (British English, South African English, and Caribbean English) or pok choi is a type of Chinese cabbage (Brassica rapa subsp.
Unlike ordinary weight loss from undereating, this illness-linked syndrome strips away muscle mass in ways good nutrition can't fully undo — what condition is it?
Cachexia is a syndrome that occurs in people with certain illnesses, causing muscle loss that cannot be fully reversed with improved nutrition.
This clouding of the eye's lens is responsible for nearly 40 percent of blindness cases worldwide, often causing halos around lights and trouble seeing at night — what condition is it?
Cataract is a cloudy area in the lens of the eye that impairs vision.
Linked to repeated head trauma, this worsening neurodegenerative disease turns up in boxers and footballers — and even in soccer players, largely from heading the ball. What is it?

Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) is a neurodegenerative disease linked to repeated trauma to the head. The encephalopathy symptoms can include behavioral problems, mood problems, and problems with thinking.
This group of mostly evergreen, cone-bearing trees and shrubs reproduces via wind-pollination, with the seeds themselves also scattered by the wind — what plant group is it?
Conifer are a group of vascular plants and a subset of gymnosperms.
Native to Mexico and Central America and related to the sunflower and daisy, this genus of 49 tuberous perennial species blooms in nearly every color except blue — which genus?
Dahlia is a genus of bushy, tuberous, herbaceous perennial plants native to Mexico and Central America.
Tamed in Africa millennia ago and still hauling loads across the developing world, which equine traces its lineage to Equus africanus?
Donkey is a domesticated equine. It was domesticated in Africa some 5000–7000 years ago, and has been used mainly as a working animal since that time.
This Russian economist served as Vladimir Putin's economic adviser before becoming governor of her country's central bank, and was ranked among Forbes' most powerful women in 2019 — who is she?
Elvira Nabiullina (born 29 October 1963) is a Russian economist and current governor of the Central Bank of Russia.
Botanists use this word for any plant whose leaves stay green and functional through every season, never going bare like a deciduous tree — what is it?
Evergreen is a plant which has foliage that remains green and functional throughout the year.
Holding doctorates in both medicine and philosophy from Pisa by age 21, this Italian naturalist became the "founder of experimental biology" by disproving spontaneous generation — who was he?
Francesco Redi (18 February 1626 - 1 March 1697) was an Italian physician, naturalist, biologist, and poet.
The tallest living land animal and the largest ruminant on Earth, this African mammal's closest living relative is the shorter-necked okapi — name the animal?
Giraffe (genus Giraffa) are large African hoofed mammals.

Rooted in a Hebrew word meaning 'to walk' or 'to go,' this collective body of Jewish religious law guides both worship and everyday life, tracing back to biblical commandments and later rabbinic codes — what is it?
Halakha (hah-), is the collective body of Jewish religious laws that are derived from the Written and Oral Torah.
Before founding his own Italian supercar company, this Argentine-Italian engineer worked for both Renault and Lamborghini — who is he?
Horacio Pagani (auto executive) (born 10 November 1955) is an Argentine-Italian businessman and automobile engineer in the automotive industry.
Its partial form is called 'subileus' — this condition describes an intestine that can't propel its contents forward, whether from a lack of peristalsis or a mechanical blockage — what is it?
Ileus is a disruption of the normal propulsive ability of the intestine.
This NASA astronaut and Marine Corps test pilot commanded the SpaceX Crew-7 mission and served as a flight engineer aboard the International Space Station — who is she?
Jasmin Moghbeli (born June 24, 1983) is an American U.S.
Brewed from the root of a Pacific pepper plant and sipped from a communal bowl in island ceremonies, this psychoactive drink takes its bitter-tasting name from Tongan and Marquesan — what is it?
Kava (Piper methysticum: Latin 'pepper' and Latinized Greek 'intoxicating') is a plant in the pepper family, native to the Pacific Islands.

A Cornell-trained engineer and Atlanta factory superintendent, this man was wrongly convicted of a young employee's murder, then kidnapped from prison and lynched in a case now central to American antisemitism — who was he?

Leo Frank (April 17, 1884 - August 17, 1915) was an American lynching victim wrongly convicted of the murder of 13-year-old Mary Phagan, an employee in a factory in Atlanta, Georgia, where he was the superintendent.
Credited as the 'Father of Cinematography' for filming Roundhay Garden Scene in Leeds in 1888, this French inventor mysteriously vanished in 1890 before cinema took off — who was he?

Louis Le Prince (28 August 1841 - disappeared 16 September 1890; declared dead 16 September 1897) was a French artist and the inventor of an early motion-picture camera, and director of Roundhay Garden Scene.
Sharing the 1963 Nobel Prize in Physics for work on nuclear shell structure, this German-American theorist became only the second woman ever to win that prize, after Marie Curie — who was she?
Maria Goeppert Mayer (ne Goppert; June 28, 1906 - February 20, 1972) was a German-American theoretical physicist who shared the 1963 Nobel Prize in Physics with J. Hans D. Jensen.
Ranked among the world's wealthiest people as of 2026, this billionaire founded and still leads a technology infrastructure giant he once took private in a landmark buyout — who is he?
Michael Dell (born February 23, 1965) is an American billionaire businessman and investor.
An Austrian-School economist who called the state 'robbery systematized and writ large,' he founded and championed anarcho-capitalism across more than twenty books — who was he?
Murray Rothbard (March 2, 1926 - January 7, 1995) was an American economist of the Austrian School, economic historian, political theorist, and activist.

Found across 26 African countries in lakes, rivers and swamps — with one of its largest undisturbed populations at Kenya's Lake Turkana — adult males of this reptile can stretch past five meters; what is it?
Nile crocodile (Crocodylus niloticus) is a large crocodilian native to freshwater habitats in Africa, where it is present in 26 countries.
Listed by Ptolemy and named for a hunter in Greek myth, this winter constellation boasts the supergiant stars Rigel and Betelgeuse and a famous short, straight line of three stars — which is it?
Orion (constellation) is a prominent set of stars visible during winter in the northern celestial hemisphere.
First domesticated in Neolithic China and rarely living past twenty years, this deciduous fruit tree also produces a smooth-skinned variety commercially sold as a different fruit — which tree?
Peach (Prunus persica) is a deciduous tree that bears edible juicy fruits with various characteristics.

This class of lipid molecules has a water-loving 'head' built around a phosphate group and two water-fearing fatty-acid 'tails' — and forms an essential building block of neuronal membranes in the brain. Name the class of molecule?

Phospholipid are a class of lipids whose molecule has a hydrophilic "head" containing a phosphate group and two hydrophobic "tails" derived from fatty acids, joined by an alcohol residue (usually a glycerol molecule).
Though it looks like a small dolphin, this cetacean is actually more closely related to narwhals and belugas, and can be told apart by its flattened, spade-shaped teeth — what animal is it?
Porpoise are small dolphin-like cetaceans classified under the family Phocoenidae.
This yellow-white fluid forms at sites of infection and inflammation — when trapped in tissue it's called an abscess, and near the skin's surface a pimple — name the substance?
Pus is an exudate, typically white-yellow, yellow, or yellow-brown, formed at the site of inflammation during infections, regardless of cause.
Named from Greek words for 'rose' and 'tree,' this genus of over 1,000 woody flowering plant species serves as the national flower of Nepal and the state flower of Washington — what is it?

Rhododendron (pl.: rhododendra), from Ancient Greek (rhdon), meaning "rose", and (dndron), meaning "tree", is a very large genus of about 1,024 species of woody plants in the heath family (Ericaceae).
Also known as Besnier-Boeck-Schaumann disease, this non-infectious condition causes inflammatory cell clusters called granulomata, most often striking the lungs, skin, or lymph nodes — what is it?
Sarcoidosis is a non-infectious granulomatous disease involving abnormal collections of inflammatory cells that form lumps known as granulomata.
This macrofungus, native to East Asia and mainland Southeast Asia, is now cultivated and consumed around the globe as one of its most widely eaten mushrooms. What mushroom is this?
Shiitake is a macrofungus native to East Asia and mainland Southeast Asia, which is cultivated and consumed around the globe.

This now-discredited scientific theory held that living creatures like fleas or maggots could regularly arise directly from non-living matter such as dust or rotting flesh, and was coherently synthesized by Aristotle. Name the theory?
Spontaneous generation is a superseded scientific theory that held that living creatures could arise from non-living matter and that such processes were commonplace and regular.
Time named this marine biologist its first "Hero for the Planet" in 1998, the same year she became a National Geographic Explorer — and she was also NOAA's first chief scientist. Who is she?
Sylvia Earle (born August 30, 1935) is an American marine biologist, oceanographer, explorer, writer, and lecturer.
Raised by a wealthy uncle after his father fled following a fight, this English philosopher laid out an influential social contract theory in his 1651 book 'Leviathan' — who is he?

Thomas Hobbes (HOBZ; 5 April 1588 - 4 December 1679) was an English philosopher and political theorist, best known for his 1651 book Leviathan, in which he expounds an influential formulation of social contract theory.
Native to Central and South America but now found in sub-Saharan Africa, which parasitic flea burrows into skin to cause the condition tungiasis?
Tunga penetrans is a species of flea also known as the jigger, jigger flea, chigoe, chigo, chigoe flea, chigo flea, nigua, sand flea, or burrowing flea.

Commanding the first spaceflight to carry multiple crew members in 1964, this Soviet cosmonaut became the first human to die during a space mission when his capsule's parachute failed on reentry in 1967 — who was he?
Vladimir Komarov (16 March 1927 - 24 April 1967) was a Soviet test pilot, aerospace engineer, and cosmonaut.
Which East Asian citrus fruit, believed to have originated in central China as a hybrid of mandarin orange and ichang papeda, is now also grown in New Zealand, Australia, and parts of Europe?
Yuzu (Citrus junos, from Japanese or) is a citrus fruit and plant in the family Rutaceae of Chinese origin.
Native to Africa and Yemen, this drought-resistant tree species has individuals radiocarbon-dated to over 1,275 years old — what is it?
Adansonia digitata: Species of plant native to Africa.
Brother of a concert pianist and son of an astronomer, this Russian mathematician built the foundational theory of stability in dynamical systems — who was he?
Formed when ammonia gains an extra hydrogen ion, this positively charged molecule, NH4+, is a key player in the global nitrogen cycle — what is it?
Caused by the bacterium Bacillus anthracis, its skin form starts as a small blister that becomes a painless ulcer with a telltale black center — what infection is this?
Anthrax: Infection caused by Bacillus anthracis bacteria. The skin form presents with a small blister with surrounding swelling that often turns into a painless ulcer with a black center.
Known as mugwort or wormwood, this daisy-family plant has long been used for both medicinal and culinary purposes — what species is it?

Artemisia vulgaris: Medicinal plant known as common mugwort. It is one of several species in the genus Artemisia commonly known as mugwort, although Artemisia vulgaris is the species most often called mugwort.
Blooming for weeks each spring and thriving in the shade under trees, these flowering shrubs belong to the genus Rhododendron — what are they called?
Azalea: Subgroup of rhododendron flowering shrubs.
Named after a barberry-related plant genus and glowing bright yellow under ultraviolet light, this alkaloid was recorded in an ancient Chinese herbal medicine text around 200 BC. What compound is it?
This crested songbird in the crow family sports a black, U-shaped collar and is known for hiding acorns to eat later — which eastern North American bird?
Blue jay: Species of bird. The blue jay (Cyanocitta cristata) is a passerine bird in the family Corvidae, native to eastern North America.

Unique among mammals, human females are the only ones to permanently develop this secondary sex organ at puberty rather than just during pregnancy, and it later produces milk via the mammary gland — which body part?
Breast: Part of the female primate torso that has mammary glands.
The fifth most abundant element in Earth's crust and a reactive alkaline earth metal, this element's name comes from the Latin word for 'lime' obtained by heating limestone — what is it?
Calcium: Chemical element with atomic number 20 (Ca)
This compound ferries long-chain fatty acids into a cell's mitochondria to be burned for energy and is naturally concentrated in muscles like the heart — what is it?
Carnitine: Compound active in mitochondria. Carnitine is a quaternary ammonium compound involved in metabolism in most mammals, plants, and some bacteria.
In calculus, this formula computes the derivative of a composite function by multiplying together the derivatives of its two component functions — what is it called?

Native to Sri Lanka, the inner bark of this evergreen tree is the original source of a beloved baking spice, sometimes distinguished from a cheaper cousin as the 'true' or 'Ceylon' variety — which tree?
Cinnamomum verum: Species of tree. The inner bark of the tree is historically regarded as the spice cinnamon, though this term was later generalized to include C. cassia as well.
Named for an Indonesian island where an 18th-century naturalist first catalogued it, this pungent, oregano-scented succulent also goes by Cuban oregano and Indian borage — which plant?
Coleus amboinicus: Species of plant. Coleus amboinicus is a species of semi-succulent perennial plant in the family Lamiaceae.
Produced mainly by the adrenal cortex and surging in response to stress and low blood sugar, this steroid hormone is sold as medicine under the name hydrocortisone — what is it?
Built from microfilaments, intermediate filaments, and microtubules, this network gives a cell its shape and lets it contract and migrate — what is it?
Cytoskeleton: Network of filamentous proteins that forms the internal framework of cells.
Carnations and sweet williams both belong to which flowering plant genus of about 340 species, native mainly to Europe and Asia?
Attracted to rotting fruit and fermenting drinks, this insect became the first animal launched into space in 1946 and has earned six Nobel Prizes for scientists who studied it — what is it?
Drosophila melanogaster: Species of fruit fly.
Native to southern India, this ginger-family plant produces the aromatic seeds used in both sweet and savory cooking — what is it, botanically?
Elettaria cardamomum: Species of flowering plant.
This fibromuscular tube carries food from throat to stomach using peristaltic contractions, and its name traces to Ancient Greek roots meaning roughly 'I carry what I ate.' What is it?
Esophagus: Vertebrate organ through which food passes to the stomach.
Carried out by the lungs, kidneys, and skin in vertebrates, this bodily process rids the body of metabolic byproducts like urea, carbon dioxide, and uric acid — what is it called?
Excretion: Elimination of metabolic waste products by an organism.
Spending 36 years at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory contributing to America's robotic space missions, which Iranian-American scientist later advised high-tech startups after retiring in 2016?
Traditionally pounded from cassava, plantains, and cocoyam, this West African staple gets a shoutout in Chinua Achebe's novel Things Fall Apart — what dish is it?
Fufu: Dough-like food in African cuisine.
Nicknamed 'The Lawyer' and once controlling over 4% of Italy's GDP as Fiat's principal shareholder, this stylish industrialist was the richest man in modern Italian history — who is he?
The seeds of five plants in this family, including rice, wheat, maize, barley, and sugar cane, cover 46% of the world's farmland — what group of plants is this?
Grass: Collective name for three families of plants.
This British mathematician has studied the math of dating and pandemics, delivered the Royal Institution's 2019 Christmas Lectures, and hosted BBC's 'Secret Genius of Modern Life' — who is she?
Hannah Fry: British mathematician and broadcaster (born 1984)
Its name Greek for 'different wings,' this insect suborder of about 40,000 species is the group most consistently termed 'true bugs' within Hemiptera — which group is it?
Heteroptera: Suborder of true bugs. The name "Heteroptera" is used in two very different ways in modern classifications.
Also known as dihydrocodeinone, this semi-synthetic opioid is often combined with acetaminophen or ibuprofen for pain and is sold alone as an extended-release drug called Zohydro ER — what is it?
Hydrocodone: Opioid drug used in pain relief.
First described to Europeans in 1812, this reddish-brown African antelope's males sport lyre-shaped horns up to three feet long — which animal?
Impala: Species of antelope found in Africa.

This Scottish physicist's equations unified electricity, magnetism, and light into a single theory — the second great unification in physics after Newton's — while also helping found statistical mechanics — who is he?
James Clerk Maxwell: Scottish physicist and mathematician (1831–1879)
Nicknamed 'Father of the National Parks,' this Scottish-born naturalist co-founded the Sierra Club and helped preserve Yosemite Valley and Sequoia National Park — who is he?
Nicknamed the 'honey bear' though unrelated to actual bears, this nocturnal rainforest mammal is the only member of its genus and a cousin of raccoons and coatis — which arboreal creature?
Closely related to earthworms but equipped with a sucker at each end, these segmented worms are mostly freshwater dwellers, and the medicinal species famously feeds on blood — what are they?
Leech: Parasitic or predatory annelid worms.
A Chinese computer engineer turned science-fiction author, he won the Hugo Award for The Three-Body Problem and the Locus Award for its sequel, Death's End. Who is he?
Liu Cixin: Chinese science fiction writer (born 1963)
Developed by MathWorks and named for its focus on matrix manipulations, this proprietary numeric computing environment powers the add-on Simulink for model-based design. What's it called?
MATLAB: Numerical computing environment and programming language.
Co-founding a company in his Harvard dorm room in February 2004, he became the world's youngest self-made billionaire at age 23. Who is he?
Mark Zuckerberg: American businessman and programmer (born 1984)
Long before chemists called it 3,4,5-trimethoxyphenethylamine, this psychedelic was drawn from peyote and San Pedro cacti for spiritual ceremonies — which naturally occurring compound is it?
Mescaline: Naturally occurring psychedelic compound. The practice of ingesting mescaline-containing cacti extracts dates back over 6,000 years.

Codenamed 'Havoc' by NATO, this Soviet tandem-seat attack helicopter carries a single gun in an under-nose barbette and, unlike its predecessor, has no secondary troop-transport role. What aircraft is this?
Mil Mi-28: Russian attack helicopter. The Mil Mi-28 (NATO reporting name "Havoc") is a Soviet heavy-weight, all-weather, day-night, tandem-seat anti-armour military attack helicopter.

This Japanese biologist used diffusion equations to calculate how likely a gene is to take over a population, and in 1968 proposed the "neutral theory" that genetic drift, not just selection, drives molecular evolution — who was he?
First identified from an 1856 fossil in a German valley, this group of archaic humans roamed Europe and Asia until vanishing around 40,000 years ago as modern humans arrived — who were they?

The first of the Century Series jet fighters, this supersonic aircraft was the U.S. Air Force's first fighter capable of level supersonic flight, first taking to the air in May 1953, seven months ahead of schedule — which jet?

North American F-100 Super Sabre: 1953 fighter aircraft family. The North American F-100 Super Sabre is an American supersonic jet fighter aircraft designed and produced by the aircraft manufacturer North American Aviation.
Named after an ancient Greek city, this cactus genus is better known by its fruit's common name, the prickly pear, and goes by nopal or sabra in other cultures — what genus is it?
Opuntia: Genus of cactus. The plant has been introduced to Australia, southern Europe, the Middle East, and parts of Africa.

Named after the bones that house them — frontal, maxillary, ethmoid, and sphenoid — these four paired air-filled spaces surround the nasal cavity and have a still-debated evolutionary purpose — what are they called?
Paranasal sinuses: Air-filled spaces surrounding the nasal cavity.
This inflammation of the sac surrounding the heart causes sharp chest pain that eases when sitting up and worsens when lying down or breathing deeply — what condition is it?
Pericarditis: Inflammation of the pericardium. Pericarditis (PER-i-kar-DYE-tis) is inflammation of the pericardium, the fibrous sac surrounding the heart.
Their name blends the Greek for "plant" and "drifter": these self-feeding plankton photosynthesize in the sunlit surface waters of oceans and lakes — what are they?
Phytoplankton: Autotrophic members of the plankton ecosystem.
Native to Southeast Asia and tasting like a sweet grapefruit, this non-hybrid citrus is the largest of them all — in fact, an ancestor of both the grapefruit and the bitter orange — what is it?
Pomelo: Citrus fruit from Southeast Asia.
Created in the early 18th century, this dark pigment was the first modern synthetic color, made by oxidizing iron ferrocyanide salts — what is it?
Prussian blue: Synthetic pigment. Prussian blue (also known as Berlin blue, Brandenburg blue, Parisian and Paris blue) is a dark blue pigment produced by oxidation of ferrous ferrocyanide salts.
Element 88 reacts with nitrogen rather than oxygen in air, turning black, and once glowed in self-luminous paints despite being highly carcinogenic — which element is it?
Radium: Chemical element with atomic number 88 (Ra)

Grown for its fleshy, edible stalks since before the 18th century in Europe and Scandinavia, this plant's broad triangular leaves are actually poisonous due to their high oxalic acid content. What is it?
Rhubarb: Species of herbaceous perennial plant with fleshy, sour edible stalks.
First identified in November 2002 and traced through civets to horseshoe bats in Yunnan, this viral respiratory disease had an 11% fatality rate before its outbreak ended in 2003 — which disease?
Creator of a satirical comic strip about corporate cubicle life, this cartoonist also wrote the pandeistic novella 'God's Debris' — who is he?
Scott Adams: American cartoonist and author (1957–2026)
